title: Higher immediate physics post-test scores with a designed AI tutor
location: Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts, United States
observed_outcome: Immediate physics test performance improved with the designed AI tutor: an adjusted effect of 0.63 standard deviations versus classroom active learning.
human_contribution: Instructors supplied curriculum, correct solutions, scaffolding, prompts, and videos. Students solved problems.
evidence_supports: Two lessons with conditions reversed between groups. Reported post-test observations: 142 AI, 174 classroom. The adjusted effect controls for prior proficiency, lesson, test version, and time on task.
limitations: One course with a test ceiling. The instructional package included self-pacing, videos, and at-home study. The comparison does not isolate generic AI or establish teacher replacement. Retention and later transfer were not measured.
tradeoffs: Any wider deployment assessment would need to consider costs, access, and the reliability of feedback.
replication_hypothesis: Test expert-designed lessons, reliable feedback, and structured practice in other populations with delayed assessments.

sources.title: AI tutoring outperforms in-class active learning: an RCT introducing a novel research-based design in an authentic educational setting

source_case_identifier: Randomized crossover study of two introductory physics lessons
benefit_summary: Immediate physics test performance improved with the designed AI tutor: an adjusted effect of 0.63 standard deviations versus classroom active learning.
stakeholder_detail: The eligible study population comprised 194 undergraduate physics students. The reported post-test counts describe observations in a crossover study, not independent parallel groups or proof that every student benefited.
